lesson_title: Crates, Shelves and the Secret Code of Plans
hook_text: A building plan is secret code with ten words — and one of them saves your back.
clip_script: Your neighbour unrolls the plan of her new granny flat and it looks like secret writing. It is — but the language has about ten words. Fat double lines: walls, and the gap between them is the wall's real thickness. A gap with a little quarter-moon: a door, and the moon shows which way it swings — so nothing bulky may stand inside that arc. Thin double lines: a window. WC: the toilet. Now the magic number: 1 to 100 — every centimetre of paper is a METRE of building. Ruler on the lounge: 50 by 40 millimetres. Real room: 5 by 4 metres. Will the 1,8-metre bookshelf fit? Draw an 18-millimetre rectangle and park it — you just moved furniture with a pencil instead of your back. But the floor plan has a blind spot: UP. For heights, walk around the paper house — the elevations stare at each wall like a neighbour. One trap: face a wall from outside and left becomes right, like an oncoming taxi whose driver appears on your left. Anchor to the compass — east never flips. Then the hardware store: 500 tiles plus ten percent is 550, boxes of twenty, buy TWENTY-EIGHT. Paint works out to 9,6 litres — buy TEN. Shops sell whole things, and the maths always rounds up.
visual_style: A rolled plan opening across a stoep table, symbols lighting up one by one with labels; a pencil bookshelf sliding along a plan wall; the flat drawing folding up into a 3D granny flat as elevations snap onto each wall; tile boxes stacking up to 28 and paint tins counting to 10.
pacing: Rapid symbol tour, a pause on the centimetre-is-a-metre reveal, playful bookshelf slide, crisp rounding-up finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any plan, match any elevation, and buy exactly enough tiles and paint.
